answer_1.quote: Transforming complex sentences into a sequence of shorter sentences, while preserving the original meaning, can facilitate the processing of complex texts for humans and machines alike. It is, for instance, an important operation in text simplification , where simpler split sentences can provide content that is easier to read and comprehend.
answer_1.outputs: Sequences of shorter sentences preserving the original meaning of complex input sentences

answer_2.quote: Following , we used three separate metrics to evaluate our models. SARI , the standard simplification metric as computed by the EASSE toolkit , which provides the proportion of n-grams that are added (add in what follows), kept (keep) or deleted (del). As a second metric, we used the normalised BertScore (hereafter, BESC) , which has proved successful to measure meaning preservation. BLEU scores, computed with sacreBLEU , are reported as well, as a precision measure of n-gram overlap between hypotheses and references. We also included an additional metric for the task to indicate output compliance (CPL), i.e. the percentage of output sequences that include at least two separate sentences, to directly identify unsplit output.

answer_4.quote: Results from two human evaluations, a comparative 3-way ranking task and a qualitative evaluation, further support our conclusions. ... For this specific evaluation, human evaluators were presented a source sentence and two SPRP hypotheses, which they had to rank in a 3-way evaluation... Additionally, we performed an additional human evaluation, this time centred on assessing the validity of individual SPRP hypotheses on a set of predefined criteria.
answer_4.guideline: Evaluators were asked to compare the hypotheses according to SPRP criteria of compliance, sensicality, grammatically, missed facts and omitted facts. ... For the qualitative evaluation, human evaluators had to answer 6 questions related to the quality of an SPRP hypothesis: Is it sensical? (scale 0-2), Grammatical? (scale 0-2), No missed facts? (Y/N), No new facts? (Y/N), Correct split? (Y/N), Enough split? (Y/N).
